newsitem.title: INDONESIA: ASEAN summit blasts Portugal, dodges Burma.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN summit blasts Portugal, dodges Burma.

text.p: Southeast Asian leaders blasted Portugal on Saturday for its confrontation with Indonesia over East Timor, but dodged the question of when to admit Burma formally to the seven-nation ASEAN grouping.
The heads of government of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) also avoided discussing forthcoming world trade talks in Singapore.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said this was because ASEAN's firm opposition to introducing what it regards as non-trade issues at the inaugural ministeral meeting of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) opening on December 8 was already well known.

Speaking at a news conference after a one-day "informal" summit, Alatas said the leaders had criticised Portugal for causing "unwarranted aggravation" in relations between ASEAN and the European Union by bringing up the issue of East Timor in talks on economic cooperation between the two regions.
ASEAN's members -- Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Singapore, the Philippines, Vietnam and Brunei -- include some of the world's fastest growing developing economies.

A joint declaration at the end of the summit said the leaders had "noted with increasing concern the efforts of one member of the EU to introduce extraneous issues such as the question of East Timor in the economic cooperation and interaction between ASEAN and the EU".

The two groupings had failed to renew an economic cooperation agreement at Portugal's demand following the 1991 killing of at least 50 demonstrators in the East Timor capital of Dili by Indonesian troops.
Indonesia invaded the former Portuguese colony in December 1975 and declared the territory its 27th province the following July in a move still not recognised by the United Nations.
The ASEAN leaders ducked the contentious question of exactly when to admit Burma to the group, saying it would join simultaneously with fellow ASEAN observers Laos and Cambodia.
The leaders said however they wanted all 10 Southeast Asian nations within ASEAN.
Laos and Cambodia had been expected to join at the annual ASEAN foreign ministers' conference being held next July in the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur on the group's 30th anniversary.
Alatas said no fixed time had been set for admitting Laos and Cambodia, but added: "You can draw your own conclusions."
Burma was admitted as an observer last July in a move that drew criticism from Western powers over Rangoon's human rights and democracy record.

Ministers on the fringe of the summit said ASEAN was determined not to allow issues like labour standards and human rights to be linked with trade at the WTO meeting in Singapore, as the United States and Norway have vocally sought to do.
